did_you_know.text: The seventh year is called shmittah in rabbinic Hebrew, from the root sh-m-t, meaning to let go or release. This is also the origin of the modern Hebrew word shmittah.
The sabbatical year is like a Sabbath for the land: not only people rest, but the soil receives a break from regular planting and pruning.
Sefiach is produce that grows by itself from seeds that fell in the field, without new planting. The Torah therefore includes natural growth in the produce of the sabbatical year.
Counting seven cycles of seven years creates 49 years, much like counting seven weeks leads to Shavuot. In both cases, the number seven builds a complete period.
The announcement of the Jubilee is set for Yom Kippur, the tenth day of the seventh month. The word yovel is probably connected with a ram’s horn, which could be used as a shofar.
The word deror means freedom or release, and similar words in ancient Near Eastern languages had a related meaning. This is the source of the biblical expression “proclaim freedom.”

The rabbis expanded the prohibition “do not wrong” beyond unfair prices: hurtful or humiliating speech was also considered ona’ah. Thus, a rule about commerce became a principle of sensitivity in human relationships.
The price is calculated by the number of harvests remaining until the Jubilee, so the transaction resembles selling the right to use the land for a limited time rather than selling it permanently.
The triple harvest of the sixth year is meant to cover the transition: the sixth year, the sabbatical year, and the time until the next crop ripens. It is a practical answer to the fear of shortage.
The verse describes a precise agricultural timetable: planting resumes in the eighth year, but people continue eating the old produce until the ninth year’s harvest arrives.
The phrase “the land is Mine” presents people not as absolute owners, but as temporary caretakers and users. This idea places limits on the power of property owners.

A house in a walled city has a different status from a field or a village house: it can be redeemed only during one year and does not return to its original owner at the Jubilee. The Torah distinguishes urban property from agricultural property.

According to the Book of Numbers, the Levites had 48 cities, including cities of refuge. These cities allowed them to live throughout the land, even though they did not receive a large tribal territory like the other Israelites.
The phrase “strengthen him” means supporting a person before he falls completely, not merely helping after he has become destitute. It is an early idea of a social support network.
The word neshekh is related to the verb “to bite,” suggesting that interest bites into the borrower’s situation. The word tarbit emphasizes the money or food that keeps increasing.
The biblical term eved can also mean a servant or worker, not always a chattel slave in the modern sense. Here the Torah limits the enslavement of an Israelite who sold himself because of poverty.
The word perekh describes harsh and crushing forced labor, and it also appears in the description of Israelite labor in Egypt. This connection warns those with power not to repeat Egypt’s pattern.
The chapter ends by recalling the Exodus, turning historical memory into a social principle: a people redeemed from slavery must not treat its own members as absolute property.
